To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the equilibrium selection in evolutionary learning is very robust to the details of the matching mechanism, and the resulting dynamics are relatively fast, as long as the probability of mutation is sufficiently small.

the equilibrium selection mechanism of the standard replicator dynamics, in a population of agents who play a symmetric 2×N game and are matched literally randomly, is the average performance of each player's strategy, and that, under this mechanism, the Pareto efficient equilibrium of the game is selected, per se, in a finite number of steps.

in symmetric 2× 2 games, the equilibrium that is selected in the limit is the Pareto-efficient (or “risk-dominant”) equilibrium, rather than the equilibrium that would be selected by a population of fully rational agents.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what happens to an economy when the agents in that economy have limited information.
the question of whether and how the equilibrium selection problem can be resolved.
the question: What are the conditions that are necessary for a particular equilibrium to be selected in an evolutionary process?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of this paper are very important and should be taken very seriously.
the results in the paper show that in the class of symmetric coordination games the Pareto efficient equilibrium is selected in the limit of zero probability of experimentation (i.e., mutation).
the model of evolutionary game dynamics with random matching is a good model of the process by which equilibria are selected.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we study a literally random (as opposed to assortative) matching mechanism, combined, with a process of learning, based on realized payoffs.
we have shown that the standard evolutionary game models, with a random matching mechanism, have a very strong tendency to select the Pareto-efficient outcome.
we have shown that the matching mechanism can be a crucial determinant of the outcome of the evolutionary game.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the matching process can play an important role in determining equilibrium selection.
the matching mechanism can be very important in determining the outcome of an evolutionary process.
, in the context of evolutionary game theory with learning, the matching mechanism is a crucial determinant of the equilibrium selection process.
